title: Cornstarch Goo
question: How can one bowl of goo swallow a slow mitten but stop a fast tap?
idea: Cornstarch goo is a crowd of tiny grains in water. A slow push gives the water time to slip aside, so the grains slide and the goo flows. A fast push jams the grains together before the water can move, so for a moment the goo acts like a solid.

curiosity.intro: Start with one bowl that is soft and hard. Then race two spoons, peek at the grains, squeeze a ball, and step onto wet sand.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you walk on wet sand, look down: does a pale ring appear around your step?

questions.question: Why does a fast smack stop at the top?
questions.notice: Compare the deep, sunk spoon with the dull dent in the other bowl.
questions.say: Most liquids, like water, stay just as runny however fast you push. Isaac Newton described that rule, so this goo is called non-Newtonian. A slow push lets it flow. A fast smack makes it act like a solid for a moment.
questions.try: Mix about 2 scoops of cornstarch with 1 scoop of water. Rest a spoon on top, then tap the goo fast with another. Which one sinks?

questions.question: What happens to the grains when you push fast?
questions.notice: Find the grains floating apart and the grains crowded into chains.
questions.say: Each cornstarch grain is so tiny that about five fit across one hair. Water sits between them like a slippery layer. A slow push lets the water slip aside. A fast push shoves the grains together before the water can move, so they lock up. Scientists call this jamming.
questions.try: Drag a spoon slowly through the goo, then quickly. Feel how much harder your arm has to work.

questions.question: Why does squeezed goo look dry?
questions.notice: Look at the dull, cracked skin of the ball and the shiny puddle beside it.
questions.say: Jammed grains need a little more room, so they poke up through the water at the surface. The skin turns dull and cracks. Stop squeezing, and the water covers them again, so the goo shines and melts.
questions.try: Roll a lump of goo between your palms, then stop and open your hands. Watch it melt and drip.

questions.question: Why does wet sand go pale around a foot?
questions.notice: Find the pale ring around the press mark in the wet sand.
questions.say: A step pushes the sand grains a little apart. Water sinks into the new gaps, so the top looks dry for a moment. Osborne Reynolds explained this in 1885 and named it dilatancy. Cornstarch goo does a quick version of the same trick.
questions.try: Next time you are at a beach, step on firm wet sand. Watch the pale ring appear, then lift your foot.

reading.title: One goo, two ways
reading.coverText: Start with a bowl that is soft and hard. Then race two spoons, and find out what tiny grains do when you push fast.

beats.title: Soft, then hard
beats.passage: Little Wonderer stirs white powder into a bowl of water. The goo looks runny, like milk. A slow mitten sinks right in. Then the little one taps it fast. Tap! Now it feels as hard as a table. Big Wonderer leans in to look. How can one bowl be soft and hard?

beats.title: Slow sinks, fast stops
beats.passage: Try two spoons. Rest one spoon on the goo and wait. It sinks slowly to the bottom. Now smack the goo with the other spoon. It stops at the top and leaves a dull dent! Most liquids act the same, fast or slow. Water does, and so does honey. This goo breaks that rule, so it is called non-Newtonian.
beats.prompt: How is the goo different from water?

foldable.heading: Slow sinks, fast stops
foldable.body: A resting spoon sinks slowly. A smacked spoon stops on top. Water never acts like that.

beats.title: Grains in a crowd
beats.passage: Cornstarch is made of tiny grains. About five could sit across one hair. In the goo, thin water sits between them. Push slowly, and the water slips aside. The grains slide past like skaters. Push fast, and the water cannot move in time. The grains crash together and lock into chains. That is called jamming.
beats.prompt: Why do the grains jam when you push fast?

foldable.heading: Grains in a crowd

beats.title: Dry, then shiny
beats.passage: Here is a clue. Squeeze a ball of goo, and its skin turns dull and cracked. It looks almost dry! Jammed grains need a little more room, so they poke up through the water. Stop squeezing, and the grains settle back. The water covers them again, and the ball melts into a shiny puddle.
beats.prompt: Why does the squeezed ball look dry?

foldable.heading: Dry, then shiny
foldable.body: Squeeze a goo ball, and it looks dry and cracked. Stop, and it melts into a shiny puddle.

beats.title: A slow ribbon
beats.passage: Back at the table, Big Wonderer lifts a spoonful. A slow ribbon drips back into the bowl. Little Wonderer reaches up to it. Now the guess changes. The goo is not two things. It is one crowd of grains in water. Gentle pushes let them slide. Quick pushes jam them, and then the jam melts away.
beats.prompt: How does the guess about the goo change?

foldable.heading: A slow ribbon
foldable.body: The goo is one crowd of grains. Gentle pushes let them slide; quick pushes jam them.

beats.title: Pale sand by the sea
beats.passage: Wet sand at the beach plays a cousin of this trick. Step on firm, wet sand, and it turns pale around your foot. Your step pushes the grains apart, so water sinks into the new gaps. Osborne Reynolds explained it in 1885. People have even run across a pool of goo. If they stop, they sink. How long can a jam last?

beats.passage: Rest one spoon on the goo, and it slowly sinks all the way to the bottom of the bowl. Smack the goo with a second spoon, and that spoon stops at the top, leaving a firm, dull dent with tiny cracks around it. Most liquids, such as water and honey, stay just as runny no matter how fast you push them. Isaac Newton described that rule long ago, so a goo that breaks it is called non-Newtonian. beats.passage: Cornstarch is made of grains so tiny that about five could sit side by side across a single hair. In the goo, a thin layer of water sits between the grains like a slippery cushion. Push slowly, and the water has time to slip aside, so the grains glide past each other like skaters. Push fast, and the grains are shoved together before the water can escape, so they rub, grip and lock into chains that carry the push down to the bottom of the bowl. Scientists call this jamming.
beats.prompt: How do the chains of grains stop a fast push?

beats.passage: Here is a clue that makes the idea easier to trust. Squeeze a ball of goo, and its skin turns dull and cracked, almost as if it were drying out. Jammed grains need a little more room, so they spread apart and poke up through the water at the surface, scattering the light. When the squeezing stops, the grains settle back, the water covers them again, and within a moment the ball slumps into a shiny puddle that drips off the saucer.
beats.prompt: Why does the ball turn shiny again?

beats.passage: Back at the table, Big Wonderer lifted a spoonful, and a slow, glossy ribbon of goo dripped back into the bowl. The little one reached up toward the ribbon, wondering how something so runny had felt so hard. Now the guess changed. The goo is not two different things at all, but one crowd of grains in water, and the push decides what it does. Gentle pushes let the grains slide, while quick pushes jam them into a solid patch that grows ahead of the push, like snow piling up in front of a shovel.
beats.prompt: How is a jam like snow in front of a shovel?

beats.passage: Wet sand at the beach plays a cousin of this trick. Step on firm, wet sand, and it turns pale around your foot for a moment. Your step pushes the grains apart, so water sinks down into the new gaps and the top looks dry. A scientist named Osborne Reynolds explained this in 1885 and called it dilatancy. People have even run across a whole pool of cornstarch goo, but anyone who stands still slowly sinks, because each jam melts in less than a second. How long could a jam be made to last?

poem.title: The Spoon They Forgot
lines: Little Wonderer mixed up a bowl full of goo,
two scoops of white powder, one splash of water too.
Push slow, and your mitten sinks down with a sigh.
Push fast, and it’s hard as a rock. My, oh my!
“It’s grains,” said the big one, “too tiny to see,
all slipping on water as slick as can be.
Go gently, they glide past each other with ease.
Go quickly, they jam like a crowd in a squeeze.”
So the little one rolled it, round, round, in a ball,
and it looked dry and cracked, like no goo at all.
But the moment it stopped, the ball came undone
and dribbled away in a puddle of fun.
“So is it a liquid, or is it a rock?”
Big Wonderer shrugged. “It depends on the knock.”
They argued till supper, both sure they were right,
while the spoon they forgot sank slowly from sight.
